studies.Authors: Kurahashi N, Iwasaki M, Sasazuki S, Otani T, Inoue M, Tsugane S, Japan Public Health Center-Based Prospective Study Group
studies.Journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
studies.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest quartile among men older than 60 years; localized prostate cancer
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Participants responded to a validated questionnaire, which included 147 food items.

sample_size.excerpt: Here, we conducted a population-based prospective study in 43,509 Japanese men ages 45 to 74 years who generally have a high intake of isoflavones and low incidence of prostate cancer. Participants responded to a validated questionnaire, which included 147 food items.

cases.excerpt: During follow-up from 1995 through 2004, 307 men were newly diagnosed with prostate cancer, of which 74 cases were advanced, 220 cases were organ localized, and 13 cases were of an undetermined stage.

effect_size.excerpt: These results were strengthened when analysis was confined to men ages >60 years, in whom isoflavones and soy food were associated with a dose-dependent decrease in the risk of localized cancer, with relative risks for men in the highest quartile of genistein, daidzein, and soy food consumption compared with the lowest of 0.52 [95% confidence interval (95% CI), 0.30-0.90], 0.50 (95% CI, 0.28-0.88), and 0.52 (95% CI, 0.29-0.90), respectively.

headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 9 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.72 (95% CI: 0.54–0.95), suggesting that genistein is associated with a lower risk of prostate cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 67.76%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
